topic: Starting to Export from India — Overview
question_it_answers: How do I start exporting from India? Where do I begin?
answer: To start exporting from India, you need to complete these steps in order: (1) Decide what you want to export and research if there are any restrictions on that product. (2) Register your business (proprietorship, partnership, or company). (3) Get a PAN (Permanent Account Number) for your business. (4) Get GST registration (GSTIN). (5) Apply for an IEC (Importer-Exporter Code) from DGFT — this is the single most important step and is mandatory. (6) Open a current bank account and get an AD Code from your bank. (7) Get RCMC (Registration-cum-Membership Certificate) from the relevant Export Promotion Council for your product sector. (8) Find a buyer abroad, negotiate price and Incoterms, and raise a Proforma Invoice. (9) Book a freight forwarder and get the cargo ready for shipping.
notes: Verify current steps on DGFT portal as procedures may be updated.

topic: Export Restrictions — Prohibited and Restricted Goods
question_it_answers: Are there any goods I cannot export from India?
answer: Goods are classified into four categories under India's Foreign Trade Policy: (1) Free — can be exported without any special permission. (2) Restricted — need a licence from DGFT to export. (3) Prohibited — cannot be exported at all (e.g. wildlife products banned under CITES, certain food grains during shortage). (4) Canalized — can only be exported through specific government agencies (e.g. some petroleum products through MMTC). Always check the current ITC (HS) Export Schedule on the DGFT website before assuming your product is freely exportable.
notes: The list of restricted/prohibited items is updated periodically. Always check the current Schedule 2 of ITC (HS) Classifications.

topic: Core Export Documents — Complete List
question_it_answers: What documents do I need to export from India? What is the full list of export documents?
answer: The standard documents for an Indian export shipment are: (1) Commercial Invoice — the main billing document showing goods, quantity, price, buyer/seller details. (2) Packing List — detailed list of what is packed in each box/container. (3) Bill of Lading (for sea) or Airway Bill (for air) — the transport document issued by the shipping line/airline. (4) Certificate of Origin — proves goods were made in India; issued by DGFT or Chamber of Commerce. (5) Shipping Bill — the customs export declaration filed on the ICEGATE portal; required for customs clearance. (6) Export Invoice (same as Commercial Invoice in most cases). (7) LC (Letter of Credit) or other payment documents if applicable. (8) GST Invoice. (9) IEC copy. Additional documents depending on product: Phytosanitary Certificate (plants/food), Quality Certificate (buyer-specified), FSSAI Certificate (food products), etc.
notes: Some buyers or destination countries require additional documents. Always confirm with your freight forwarder.

topic: Shipping Bill — Customs Export Declaration
question_it_answers: What is a Shipping Bill and how do I file it?
answer: A Shipping Bill is the mandatory customs document that every Indian exporter must file to get customs clearance for an export shipment. It is filed electronically on the ICEGATE portal (https://www.icegate.gov.in). Types of Shipping Bills: (1) Free Shipping Bill — for freely exportable goods, no incentive claim. (2) Dutiable Shipping Bill — if export duty is applicable on your product. (3) Drawback Shipping Bill — to claim Duty Drawback (a refund of customs duties paid on imported inputs). (4) DEPB Shipping Bill — if claiming DEPB (Duty Entitlement Passbook, now discontinued). Once filed and assessed by customs, the Bill gives 'Let Export' order, after which goods can be physically loaded. Your Customs House Agent (CHA) / Customs Broker normally handles this filing on your behalf.
notes: IEC number must be linked to ICEGATE before filing.

topic: Certificate of Origin
question_it_answers: What is a Certificate of Origin and do I need one?
answer: A Certificate of Origin (COO) is a document that certifies that your exported goods were manufactured/produced in India. It is required by many importing countries to determine import duties and to comply with trade agreement rules. Types: (1) Non-preferential COO — general proof of origin, issued by Chambers of Commerce (e.g. FICCI, CII, local Chambers). (2) Preferential COO — issued when exporting under a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) to claim lower/zero import duty in the destination country. These are issued by DGFT. Example: If exporting to the UAE under India-UAE CEPA, a preferential COO lets the UAE importer pay lower duty. Check whether your destination country has an FTA with India at the DGFT website.
notes: FTA list changes as new agreements are signed. Verify current FTAs on DGFT.

topic: IEC Registration — What It Is and How to Get It
question_it_answers: What is an IEC and how do I get one?
answer: An Importer-Exporter Code (IEC) is a 10-digit number issued by DGFT (Directorate General of Foreign Trade). It is mandatory for any business or individual who wants to export or import goods from India — no export shipment can legally leave without one. How to apply: (1) Go to https://www.dgft.gov.in. (2) Click 'Apply for IEC' under Services. (3) Documents needed: PAN card, business address proof, bank account details (cancelled cheque or bank certificate). (4) Fee: ₹500 (online payment). (5) Time: typically 2–3 working days (fully online, no physical visit needed). The IEC has no expiry but must be confirmed annually (a free, one-minute online step on DGFT portal) or it gets deactivated.
notes: Annual update/confirmation is mandatory. Fee and processing time should be re-verified on DGFT before advising.

topic: GST and Export — Zero-Rated Supply, LUT, IGST Refund
question_it_answers: Do I need GST registration to export? What is GST's role in exports?
answer: Yes, GST registration (GSTIN) is required before you can export. Exports are treated as 'zero-rated supplies' under the IGST Act — meaning you don't charge GST to foreign buyers, and you can claim a refund of GST paid on inputs (raw materials, packing, services used to make the exported goods). Two main approaches: (1) Export under LUT (Letter of Undertaking) — you don't pay IGST at export time, and later claim a refund of input tax credit. This is the most common approach for regular exporters. Apply for LUT on the GST portal before your first export. (2) Export with IGST payment — you pay IGST on the export value, then claim a full cash refund. The LUT route is generally preferred because it avoids blocking cash in GST payments.
source_name: CBIC — GST on Exports: Zero-Rated Supply Guidelines
notes: LUT must be renewed every financial year on the GST portal.

topic: AD Code — What It Is and Why You Need It
question_it_answers: What is an AD Code and how do I get it?
answer: AD Code (Authorised Dealer Code) is a 14-digit code assigned by your bank (Authorised Dealer bank — any bank authorised by RBI to deal in foreign exchange). It links your bank account to ICEGATE so that export payment realisation (receiving foreign currency from buyer) can be monitored. Why you need it: The Shipping Bill filed on ICEGATE must contain your AD Code, otherwise customs clearance won't proceed. How to get it: (1) Go to your bank's export/forex department. (2) Submit a request letter with your IEC number and bank account details. (3) The bank registers your AD Code at the customs port(s) you will export from. (4) No fee — the bank does this as part of their trade finance service. Each export port where you ship from needs the AD Code registered separately.
source_name: RBI — Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) Guidelines for Exporters
notes: The AD Code must be registered at each port you intend to export from. Your Customs Broker can help with port registration.

topic: RCMC — What It Is and Which Council to Join
question_it_answers: What is RCMC and which export promotion council should I join?
answer: RCMC (Registration-cum-Membership Certificate) is a certificate issued by Export Promotion Councils (EPCs) that allows you to claim export benefits and incentives under India's Foreign Trade Policy. Without RCMC, you cannot claim scheme benefits like RoDTEP, Advance Authorisation, etc. Which council to join depends on your product: Textiles & apparel → AEPC. Handicrafts → EPCH. Engineering goods → EEPC India. Chemicals → CHEMEXCIL. Pharmaceuticals → Pharmexcil. Spices → Spices Board. Coffee → Coffee Board. Gems & Jewellery → GJEPC. If no specific EPC exists for your product → FIEO (Federation of Indian Export Organisations). How to apply: Apply online through the respective EPC's website. You need your IEC number to apply. Fee and membership duration vary by council.
source_name: DGFT Foreign Trade Policy — RCMC Requirements
notes: Check the current Foreign Trade Policy for mandatory vs optional RCMC requirements by product category.

topic: HS Code — What It Is and How to Find Yours
question_it_answers: What is an HS code and how do I find the right one for my product?
answer: HS Code (Harmonised System Code) is an internationally standardised 8-digit code (in India, the ITC-HS code) that classifies every traded product. It is used on the Shipping Bill and by customs to determine: (1) Export duty (if any). (2) Import duty in the destination country. (3) Whether restrictions apply to the product. The first 6 digits are the same worldwide (international HS); India adds 2 more digits for national classification. How to find your HS code: (1) Use the ICEGATE HS code search at https://www.icegate.gov.in. (2) Describe your product clearly (material, use, form — e.g. 'handwoven cotton bedsheet, not printed'). (3) Verify the code with a Customs Broker before using it on shipping documents. Warning: An incorrect HS code can lead to customs delays, wrong duty calculation, or even a violation notice. When in doubt, get a 'Tariff Ruling' from customs.
notes: HS codes are revised periodically (last major revision: HS 2022). Always confirm against the latest schedule.

topic: HS Code — Common Categories for Indian Exports
question_it_answers: What are the HS codes for common Indian export products like textiles, spices, or handicrafts?
answer: Common HS code chapters for major Indian export categories: Textiles (Chapter 50–63): Cotton fabric (Chapter 52), Woven apparel (Chapter 62), Knitted apparel (Chapter 61), Made-up articles/bedsheets (Chapter 63). Spices (Chapter 09): Pepper (0904), Cardamom (0908), Turmeric (0910). Leather & footwear (Chapter 41–64). Gems & Jewellery (Chapter 71). Engineering goods: Iron/Steel (Chapter 72–73), Machinery (Chapter 84–85). Pharmaceuticals (Chapter 30). Food products: Rice (1006), Wheat (1001), Mango pulp (2007), Tea (0902). These are top-level chapter codes — the full 8-digit ITC-HS code for your specific product must be looked up on ICEGATE or confirmed with a Customs Broker.
notes: Always use the 8-digit ITC-HS code (not just the chapter) on shipping documents.

topic: Incoterms — Overview and Which to Use
question_it_answers: What are Incoterms and which one should I use as an Indian exporter?
answer: Incoterms (International Commercial Terms) are a set of 11 internationally recognised trade rules published by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC). They define who (exporter or importer) is responsible for: costs (freight, insurance, duties), risk of loss/damage, and documentation at each stage of the shipment. The most commonly used Incoterms for Indian exporters: FOB (Free on Board) — you handle everything until goods are loaded on the ship. The buyer pays ocean freight and insurance. Very common for sea shipments. CIF (Cost, Insurance & Freight) — you pay for ocean freight and insurance to destination port. Higher selling price, but you control logistics. EXW (Ex-Works) — you only make goods available at your factory. Buyer handles everything. Good for experienced buyers. DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) — you handle everything including import duties in the buyer's country. Maximum responsibility for the exporter. For first-time exporters, FOB or CIF are the most straightforward and widely understood.
notes: Always specify the Incoterm version (e.g. 'FOB Mumbai, Incoterms 2020') on your commercial invoice and contract.

topic: FOB — Free on Board Explained
question_it_answers: What does FOB mean? What does FOB Mumbai mean?
answer: FOB (Free on Board) means: the exporter is responsible for all costs and risks until the goods are loaded onto the ship at the named port. After loading, the buyer takes over all costs and risks. Example — FOB Mumbai: You (exporter in India) pay for: packing, transport to Mumbai port, port charges, export customs clearance. Risk transfers to buyer when goods are loaded on the vessel at Mumbai. Buyer pays: ocean freight from Mumbai to destination, marine insurance, import customs clearance and duties at destination. FOB is one of the most commonly negotiated terms for sea shipments. It gives the buyer control over the main freight leg (they often have volume discounts with their preferred shipping lines), while keeping the exporter's responsibility clear and manageable.
notes: FOB should only be used for sea/inland waterway transport, not air freight. For air, use FCA instead.

topic: CIF — Cost, Insurance and Freight Explained
question_it_answers: What does CIF mean?
answer: CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) means: the exporter pays for the cost of goods, ocean freight to the destination port, and a minimum level of marine insurance. Risk, however, transfers to the buyer when goods are loaded on the ship at the origin port (same as FOB). So under CIF: You (exporter) pay: freight to destination port + insurance + all export-side costs. Buyer pays: import duties, local delivery from destination port onward. Risk transfer: same point as FOB — when goods cross the ship's rail at origin. Important: CIF results in a higher invoice value (since freight and insurance are included in the price), which means higher customs duty for the buyer in the destination country (duty is typically calculated on CIF value). Buyers who are sensitive to import duty costs sometimes prefer FOB for this reason.
notes: Only use CIF for sea shipments. For all modes of transport, the equivalent term is CIP.

topic: Export Customs Clearance — How It Works
question_it_answers: How does export customs clearance work in India?
answer: Export customs clearance in India has the following steps: (1) Prepare documents: Commercial Invoice, Packing List, IEC, Shipping Bill data, GST invoice. (2) File Shipping Bill on ICEGATE: Done by your Customs House Agent (CHA/Customs Broker) electronically. (3) Customs Assessment: Customs officer reviews the Shipping Bill. It is either 'Out of Charge' (cleared without physical exam) or sent for examination. (4) Physical Examination (if selected): Customs officer examines the cargo at the Container Freight Station (CFS) or port. (5) Let Export Order: Once cleared, customs gives 'Let Export' order. (6) Loading: Cargo is loaded on the vessel/aircraft. (7) EGM (Export General Manifest): Shipping line files this after the ship sails — this is required for claiming GST refunds and Duty Drawback. Tip: Hire a licensed Customs Broker (also called CHA — Custom House Agent) for your first few shipments — they handle ICEGATE filing and know port procedures.
notes: The Risk Management System (RMS) at customs determines which shipments get physical examination vs auto-cleared. First-time exporters may see higher examination rates.

topic: Customs Broker / CHA — Role and When to Use One
question_it_answers: Do I need a customs broker to export? What does a customs broker do?
answer: A Customs Broker (also called CHA — Custom House Agent) is a licensed professional who files export/import documents with customs on your behalf. In India, CHAs must be licensed by CBIC. What a CHA does for you: Files the Shipping Bill on ICEGATE. Handles customs queries and inspections. Coordinates with the port/CFS for cargo movement. Ensures all documents are in order. When you must use a CHA: For most exporters, especially first-timers, using a CHA is highly recommended (though technically not legally mandatory for all shipments, practically it is almost essential because ICEGATE filing requires knowledge of customs procedures and codes). Cost: CHAs charge a service fee per shipment — typically ₹2,000–₹8,000 depending on the shipment size and port. This is a legitimate cost of exporting. How to find a licensed CHA: Check the CBIC website's list of licensed CHAs, or ask your freight forwarder for a recommendation.
notes: Verify CHA's CBIC licence number before engaging them.

topic: Freight Forwarder — What They Do
question_it_answers: What is a freight forwarder and do I need one?
answer: A freight forwarder is a company that organises the transportation of your goods from India to the buyer's location. They act as your logistics manager. What they do: Book space on ships or aircraft. Arrange container stuffing (packing into containers). Coordinate with the port, CFS, and shipping line. Often also provide customs brokerage (CHA) services or work with a CHA partner. Handle the Bill of Lading or Airway Bill. Provide freight quotes (comparing sea vs air). Do you need one? For most exporters, yes — especially in the beginning. Managing all logistics directly is complex. A good freight forwarder handles the entire movement chain. Cost: Freight forwarders typically charge freight (the actual shipping cost) + handling fee. Get quotes from 2–3 freight forwarders before deciding. Tip: For small exporters, using the buyer's nominated freight forwarder (under FOB terms) is common — the buyer books their preferred freight forwarder and you just make the goods available at port.
notes: Choose a freight forwarder with experience in your product type and destination country.

topic: Letter of Credit (LC) — What It Is and How It Works
question_it_answers: What is a Letter of Credit and how does it protect me as an exporter?
answer: A Letter of Credit (LC) is a payment guarantee issued by the buyer's bank, promising that the exporter will be paid, provided the exporter presents the correct shipping documents to the bank within the specified time. How it works: (1) Buyer's bank issues the LC and sends it to your bank in India. (2) You ship the goods and collect all required documents (Invoice, Packing List, Bill of Lading, Certificate of Origin, etc. — exactly as listed in the LC). (3) You present these documents to your Indian bank (the 'negotiating bank'). (4) If documents match the LC terms, your bank pays you (and recovers from the buyer's bank). Why it protects you: You are paid by a bank, not just relying on the buyer's goodwill. Even if the buyer goes bankrupt, the bank is still liable. Risk level: Safest payment method for the exporter (after advance payment). Key risk: If even one document doesn't exactly match the LC terms (a 'discrepancy'), your bank may not pay you. Always read the LC carefully before shipping.
source_name: RBI — Foreign Exchange Management: Export of Goods and Services
notes: LC terms are governed by UCP 600 (ICC rules). Exporters should understand key LC terms before agreeing to one.

topic: Export Payment Methods — Comparison
question_it_answers: What are the different ways I can receive payment from a foreign buyer? Which is safest?
answer: Export payment methods ranked from safest to riskiest for the exporter: (1) Advance Payment (100% upfront) — Safest for exporter. Buyer pays in full before shipment. Risk to buyer is high, so usually only trusted/established exporters get this. (2) Letter of Credit (LC) — Very safe for exporter. Bank guarantees payment if documents are correct. Best for large orders with new buyers. (3) Documents Against Payment (DP) — Bank releases shipping documents to buyer only when buyer pays. Buyer can inspect documents but only gets goods after paying. Moderate risk. (4) Documents Against Acceptance (DA) — Bank releases documents when buyer accepts a bill of exchange (a promise to pay later, e.g. 60/90 days). Risk: buyer takes goods and may default on payment. Higher risk. (5) Open Account — You ship goods and invoice the buyer. They pay after 30/60/90 days on trust. Riskiest for exporter — used only with long-trusted buyers. All export payments must come through banking channels (not cash) and must be realised within the time limit set by RBI (currently within 9 months of shipment).
source_name: RBI — Export Payment and Realisation Guidelines
notes: RBI periodically updates payment realisation timelines. Verify current limit (9 months as of 2026) on RBI website.

topic: FEMA — Foreign Exchange Compliance for Exporters
question_it_answers: What are the RBI/FEMA rules for receiving export payments?
answer: Under FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act), Indian exporters must follow these rules for export payment: (1) Realisation period: Export payment must be received within 9 months from the date of shipment (extended for certain categories like project exports). (2) Banking channels: All export payments must come through a bank (Authorised Dealer bank). Cash payments for exports are not permitted under FEMA. (3) BRC (Bank Realisation Certificate): After payment is received, your bank issues a BRC. This is required for GST refund claims and for claiming export incentives. Keep all BRCs. (4) Export Declaration Form: For shipments above USD 25,000 (approx.), the exporter must submit an Export Declaration Form (EDF) to the Authorised Dealer bank. (5) Failure to realise payment within the time limit is a FEMA violation and can attract penalties.
notes: The 9-month realisation period can be extended with AD Bank / RBI approval in genuine cases.

topic: RoDTEP Scheme — Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products
question_it_answers: What is RoDTEP? Am I eligible for it?
answer: RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products) is India's current main export incentive scheme. It refunds embedded taxes and duties (not covered by other schemes) that are incurred on the production of exported goods — such as electricity duty, VAT on fuel, mandi tax, etc. Key points: (1) Replaces the old MEIS scheme (which was found to be WTO-non-compliant). (2) The refund is given as a transferable e-scrip (an electronic credit) that can be used to pay customs duty or sold to another importer. (3) Rates vary by HS code and product — typically 0.3% to 4.3% of FOB value. (4) Claimed automatically when you file a Shipping Bill on ICEGATE (you tick the RoDTEP claim option). (5) Not all products are covered — check the schedule on the DGFT/CBIC website. Who is eligible: Most manufactured exporters are eligible. Some sectors (e.g. steel, pharmaceutical, chemicals) have specific rates. Check the RoDTEP rate for your ITC-HS code.
source_name: CBIC — RoDTEP Scheme Guidelines and Rate Schedule
notes: RoDTEP rates are revised periodically. Always verify current rate for your specific ITC-HS code.

topic: Duty Drawback Scheme
question_it_answers: What is Duty Drawback and how do I claim it?
answer: Duty Drawback is a refund of customs duties paid on imported raw materials or inputs that were used to manufacture the exported goods. In plain terms: if you imported fabric, paid customs duty, made garments, and exported them — you get back a portion of the customs duty you paid on the imported fabric. Two types: (1) All Industry Rate (AIR) — pre-fixed drawback rates by product category, applied automatically when you file the Shipping Bill. Easy to use. (2) Brand Rate — a specific rate calculated for your particular manufacturing process if AIR doesn't fairly cover your actual duty payment. More complex to apply. How to claim AIR: Choose the 'Drawback Shipping Bill' on ICEGATE when filing. The drawback amount is credited to your bank account after the EGM is filed. Timeline: Typically 3–4 weeks after shipment. Note: You cannot claim both Duty Drawback and IGST refund on the same inputs — choose one.
source_name: CBIC — Duty Drawback Rules and All Industry Rate Schedule
notes: All Industry Rates are revised annually, usually in September/October. Check current rates before estimating your refund.

topic: Advance Authorisation Scheme
question_it_answers: What is the Advance Authorisation scheme?
answer: The Advance Authorisation (AA) scheme allows Indian exporters to import raw materials, components, or inputs duty-free (zero customs duty), provided those inputs are used to manufacture and export the final product. In plain terms: you get permission to import inputs without paying customs duty, on the condition that you will export finished goods within a set time period. Key conditions: (1) The inputs imported and the exported product must follow the Standard Input-Output Norms (SION) set by DGFT. (2) Export must be completed within 18 months of import (extensions available). (3) If you don't export within the timeline, you must pay back the customs duty with interest. How to apply: Apply on the DGFT portal for an Advance Authorisation licence. Need RCMC and IEC. Best for: Exporters who use significant quantities of imported inputs and want to improve cost competitiveness.
source_name: DGFT — Advance Authorisation Scheme, Foreign Trade Policy
notes: SION norms define how much of each input is allowed per unit of export. Check applicable SION for your product on DGFT.

topic: Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) Scheme
question_it_answers: What is EPCG and how can I benefit from it?
answer: The EPCG (Export Promotion Capital Goods) scheme allows exporters to import capital goods (machinery, equipment used for manufacturing) at zero or reduced customs duty, in exchange for an export obligation. The export obligation is typically 6 times the duty saved, to be fulfilled over 6 years. Example: If you import machinery worth ₹1 crore and the customs duty would have been ₹20 lakhs — you get the duty waived. In exchange, you must export goods worth ₹1.2 crore (6x of ₹20 lakhs) within 6 years. Good for: Manufacturers who want to modernise their production equipment without paying heavy import duties, and who are confident they can meet the export obligation. How to apply: Apply on the DGFT portal for an EPCG licence.
source_name: DGFT — EPCG Scheme, Foreign Trade Policy
notes: EPCG export obligations are monitored. Non-fulfilment attracts duty recovery + interest. Plan carefully before applying.

topic: FSSAI Export Certificate for Food Products
question_it_answers: Do I need FSSAI approval to export food products from India?
answer: Yes. For exporting any food product from India, FSSAI (Food Safety and Standards Authority of India) certification/registration is required. What you need: (1) FSSAI Registration or Licence: All food businesses in India (including exporters) must have this. Type depends on turnover: State licence for turnover up to ₹20 crore; Central licence for above ₹20 crore or for manufacturing/export. (2) Health Certificate (for some countries): FSSAI issues health/sanitary certificates for exported food products, required by many importing countries. (3) Product-specific approvals: Some food products need additional approvals — e.g. organic products need NOP/EU certification; meat products need APEDA approval. Important: Many countries (US, EU, Japan) have their own food safety requirements in addition to FSSAI. Check the destination country's import requirements for your specific food product.
source_name: FSSAI — Export Certification and Food Safety Standards
notes: APEDA (Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority) handles certification for agricultural exports. Check APEDA at https://apeda.gov.in

topic: BIS Certification for Export
question_it_answers: Do I need BIS certification to export?
answer: BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) certification is generally required for exporting products that fall under compulsory BIS certification categories in India. However, for exports, there is some nuance: (1) If your product is compulsorily BIS-certified for domestic sale in India (e.g. certain electrical goods, steel products, cement), the same certification applies to exported products unless an exemption is granted. (2) For export only (products not sold domestically), some exemptions exist — check with BIS. (3) The importing country will have its own standards certification requirements (e.g. CE marking for the EU, FCC for the US, PSI for Saudi Arabia). These are often more important for exports than Indian BIS certification. Bottom line: Check both Indian BIS requirements (for your product category) AND the destination country's mandatory product standards.
notes: BIS mandatory certification lists are expanded periodically. Verify if your product has recently been added.

topic: Phytosanitary Certificate for Agricultural/Plant Exports
question_it_answers: What is a Phytosanitary Certificate and do I need one for my agricultural export?
answer: A Phytosanitary Certificate is an official document issued by the Plant Quarantine Authority (Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India) certifying that your plant-based products (fruits, vegetables, grains, seeds, plant-based products) are free from pests, diseases, and meet the plant health standards required by the importing country. Who needs it: Any exporter of fresh fruits, vegetables, seeds, grains, plant products, or wooden packaging materials. How to get it: Apply to the Plant Quarantine Station (PQS) at your nearest port/airport. The PQS officer inspects the consignment before issuing the certificate. It must be obtained before the shipment leaves India. Website: https://plantquarantineindia.nic.in. Note: Different countries have different pest-free requirements. The importing country specifies what it needs — check with the importing country's plant health authority or your buyer.
source_name: Ministry of Agriculture — Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order
notes: Some countries have additional fumigation requirements (e.g. methyl bromide treatment). Check destination country requirements.

topic: Exporting to the USA — Key Requirements
question_it_answers: What does the USA require to import goods from India? What are the US import requirements?
answer: Key requirements for exporting to the USA: (1) FDA Approval: Food, beverage, pharmaceutical, medical device, and cosmetic products must be registered with the US FDA. Prior Notice must be given to FDA before food shipment arrives. (2) Customs Entry: Filed with US CBP (Customs and Border Protection). For informal entries (below USD 2,500 per shipment), simplified process. Formal entries (above USD 2,500) need a licensed Customs Broker in the US. (3) HS code (HTS code in US terminology): Your product must be classified under the US Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS). (4) Labelling: US has specific labelling requirements (country of origin, weight in US measurements, etc.). (5) CBP Trade Partner Requirements: Importers must have an EIN/Importer number. (6) FCC Certification: Required for electronics and radio-frequency devices. (7) No active trade sanctions against India — but check latest CBP guidelines for your product. Tip: The US does not have a comprehensive FTA with India, so regular MFN (Most Favoured Nation) duty rates apply.
source_name: US CBP — Importing into the United States
notes: US import regulations change frequently. Always verify with a US-licensed Customs Broker for your specific product.

topic: Exporting to the European Union — Key Requirements
question_it_answers: What does the EU require to import goods from India?
answer: Key requirements for exporting to the EU: (1) CE Marking: Mandatory for many product categories (electronics, machinery, toys, medical devices) — confirms the product meets EU safety standards. Without CE mark, these products cannot enter the EU. (2) REACH Compliance: For chemicals and products containing chemicals — the EU REACH regulation requires safety data and registration. (3) Food Safety: Products must comply with EU food safety standards. The TRACES system is used for health certificates. (4) GSP+ / Generalised System of Preferences: India benefits from reduced EU import duties under the GSP scheme on many products. (5) Product Standards: Many EU member states require compliance with relevant EN (European Norm) standards. (6) Customs Entry: Through EU Customs Union — once cleared in any EU country, goods can move freely within the EU. (7) EUDR (EU Deforestation Regulation): From 2025, certain products (wood, coffee, soya, palm oil, leather, cocoa, rubber) must prove they are not linked to deforestation. This is a new and important requirement to check.
source_name: European Commission — Trade Helpdesk for India
notes: India-EU FTA negotiations are ongoing. If concluded, duty benefits will change significantly.

topic: Exporting to the UAE — India-UAE CEPA
question_it_answers: What are the requirements to export to UAE? Is there an FTA between India and UAE?
answer: India and UAE signed a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) effective from May 2022. This is very beneficial for Indian exporters: Key benefits of India-UAE CEPA: Over 97% of Indian goods can now enter UAE at zero duty (compared to the normal 5% UAE customs duty). To claim zero duty: You need a Preferential Certificate of Origin (COO) issued by DGFT. The product must satisfy Rules of Origin (a minimum level of Indian value-added content). General UAE import requirements: (1) Commercial Invoice and Packing List. (2) Certificate of Origin (preferential for CEPA benefit). (3) Halal Certificate for food, meat, and many personal care products — this is essential for UAE market. (4) Dubai Municipality approval for food products. (5) Products must meet UAE GSO (Gulf Standards Organisation) standards for relevant categories. The UAE is India's second-largest export destination. High-demand products: gems & jewellery, petroleum products, engineering goods, textiles, food.
source_name: DGFT — India-UAE CEPA Details and COO Guidelines
notes: Rules of Origin under CEPA vary by product. Verify for your specific HS code before claiming CEPA benefits.

topic: Trade Data Sources — Where to Find Export Statistics
question_it_answers: Which countries are importing Indian goods? Where can I find trade statistics?
answer: Key sources of Indian trade data and statistics: (1) DGFT — Foreign Trade Statistics: https://www.dgft.gov.in — quarterly and annual export data by product and country. (2) DGCI&S (Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics): http://www.dgciskol.gov.in — detailed monthly trade statistics. (3) UN Comtrade: https://comtrade.un.org — free global trade data showing what every country imports and exports, searchable by HS code. Extremely useful for market research. (4) ITC Trade Map: https://www.trademap.org — free (after registration) tool from the International Trade Centre showing market trends, top importers, prices, and competitors for any product. (5) APEDA — For agricultural products, APEDA provides destination-specific trade data. (6) Export Promotion Councils — Sector-specific data (e.g. EEPC for engineering, GJEPC for gems/jewellery). For a first-time exporter: ITC Trade Map is often the most useful — type in your HS code and see which countries are the top importers of your product type.
source_name: DGCI&S / UN Comtrade / ITC Trade Map
notes: Trade data is typically 6–12 months delayed. Use it for trend analysis, not real-time pricing.

topic: Top Indian Export Sectors and Destinations
question_it_answers: What are India's top export products and destinations?
answer: India's top export categories (as of 2024-25): (1) Petroleum products — largest category. (2) Engineering goods — machinery, iron/steel, automotive parts. (3) Gems & Jewellery — diamonds, gold jewellery. (4) Pharmaceuticals — generics for global markets. (5) Chemical products. (6) Textiles and ready-made garments. (7) Agricultural/processed food — rice, spices, meat, marine products. (8) Electronic goods — growing rapidly. India's top export destinations: USA (largest), UAE (second), Netherlands (key European hub), China, Bangladesh, UK, Germany, Singapore, Hong Kong, Belgium. India's merchandise exports were approximately USD 437 billion in FY2024. India has active FTAs with: UAE (CEPA, 2022), Australia (ECTA, 2022), Mauritius, ASEAN countries, South Korea, Japan, Sri Lanka, SAPTA (South Asian countries).
notes: Export figures change annually. Verify latest year data from DGCI&S.

topic: India International Trade Fair (IITF)
question_it_answers: What is India International Trade Fair? How do I participate?
answer: India International Trade Fair (IITF) is India's largest trade fair, held annually in November at Pragati Maidan, New Delhi. It is organised by ITPO (India Trade Promotion Organisation). Key details: When: Every year, November 14–27. Where: Bharat Mandapam / Pragati Maidan, New Delhi. Who participates: Exporters, domestic manufacturers, state pavilions, international pavilions. For exporters, IITF is useful for domestic buyer/importer meetings and for showcasing products. How to exhibit: Apply through ITPO (https://www.indiatradefair.com). Booking opens several months in advance. MSME exporters get subsidised rates for stalls. Other major Indian trade fairs by sector: AEPC fashion fairs (textiles). IIJS (India International Jewellery Show) — Gems & Jewellery. Auto Expo (automotive). Agrotech (agriculture). CAPEXIL exhibitions (chemicals).
notes: Exact dates and participation terms change annually. Check ITPO website for current year details.

topic: Government Support for Trade Fair Participation
question_it_answers: Does the government help exporters attend international trade fairs?
answer: Yes. The Government of India subsidises Indian exporters' participation in international trade fairs through the MAI (Market Access Initiative) scheme and through Export Promotion Councils. What is available: (1) MAI Scheme (DGFT): Provides financial assistance for participation in international trade fairs/exhibitions in target countries. Covers stall rental costs partially. (2) Export Promotion Councils (EPCs): Each council organises delegations to international fairs in their sector and provides subsidised participation for members. Example: EEPC takes engineering goods exporters to Hannover Messe, Germany. (3) FIEO: Organises 'Buyer-Seller Meets' in various countries where Indian exporters meet pre-qualified foreign buyers — often more targeted and cost-effective than a trade fair. How to find upcoming events: Check your relevant EPC's website and DGFT's MAI scheme portal.
notes: MAI scheme eligibility and funding amounts change with each Foreign Trade Policy cycle. Verify current terms on DGFT.

topic: FAQ — IEC Number Lookup
question_it_answers: How do I check or find my IEC number?
answer: You can look up any IEC number (your own or a potential partner's) on the DGFT website: Go to https://www.dgft.gov.in → Services → IEC Enquiry. Enter the IEC number or the company name/PAN to search. If you've lost your IEC: Log in to your DGFT account (the same account used to apply) and download the IEC certificate. If you no longer have access to your account, contact your nearest DGFT Regional Office.

topic: FAQ — Can an Individual/Sole Proprietor Export?
question_it_answers: Can I export as an individual or sole proprietor, not a company?
answer: Yes, absolutely. You do not need to be a registered company to export from India. Individuals, sole proprietors, partnership firms, LLPs, and companies can all get an IEC and export. For a sole proprietor: Use your personal PAN (or business PAN if you have one). Register for GST if your turnover is above ₹20 lakh/year (or lower thresholds for some states/goods). Apply for IEC in your name or business name. Practical note: For larger buyers (especially foreign buyers), they often prefer dealing with a registered company (Pvt Ltd or LLP) for credibility and liability reasons. But for starting out, a sole proprietorship or partnership is perfectly fine and much simpler to set up.

topic: FAQ — Export of Services vs Goods
question_it_answers: I provide IT/software services to foreign clients. Is that considered an export? Do I need IEC?
answer: Yes, providing services to foreign clients (IT, software, consulting, design, legal, etc.) is considered 'export of services' under Indian law. Key points: (1) IEC: Not mandatory for export of services only (no physical goods crossing the border). However, it is still recommended to get an IEC for future flexibility. (2) GST: Service exports are zero-rated (same as goods exports). You can export services under LUT and claim input tax credit refunds. (3) FEMA: Payment for services must come through banking channels (bank transfer) and must be received within the RBI-specified timeframe. (4) SOFTEX Form: For software/IT exports (code, services, SaaS), you must file a SOFTEX Form with RBI through the STPI (Software Technology Parks of India) or your Authorised Dealer bank. This is a regulatory requirement under FEMA. Failure to file SOFTEX is a compliance violation.
source_name: RBI — FEMA Service Export and SOFTEX Regulations
notes: SOFTEX must be filed for each software export project/contract. Verify current process with your AD Bank.

topic: FAQ — What is APEDA?
question_it_answers: What is APEDA and do I need to register with it?
answer: APEDA (Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority) is a government body under the Ministry of Commerce that promotes and regulates export of agricultural products, processed food, and fresh produce from India. Who must register with APEDA: Any exporter of APEDA-scheduled products (fresh fruits & vegetables, cereals, processed food, meat, poultry, dairy, marine products, floral products, etc.) must register with APEDA before exporting. Registration is mandatory — not optional — for covered products. How to register: Apply online at https://apeda.gov.in. You need your IEC number to apply. Fee: ₹5,000 one-time registration fee. What APEDA provides: Registration-cum-Membership Certificate (RCMC) for agri products. Financial assistance for packaging development, quality upgrades, trade fairs. Market development support.
source_name: APEDA — Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority
notes: The list of APEDA-scheduled products is defined in the APEDA Act. Check if your product is included.

topic: FAQ — What is FIEO?
question_it_answers: What is FIEO and how can it help me as an exporter?
answer: FIEO (Federation of Indian Export Organisations) is the apex body of Indian exporters, set up by the Ministry of Commerce. It is not a government body itself but is officially recognised and funded by the government. How FIEO helps exporters: (1) RCMC: If your product has no specific Export Promotion Council, FIEO issues your RCMC (needed for scheme benefits). (2) Training and mentoring: Runs export training programmes, workshops, and mentoring for new exporters. (3) Buyer-Seller Meets: Organises meetings between Indian exporters and verified foreign buyers. (4) Market information: Publishes trade alerts, country profiles, and market briefs. (5) Trade fair representation: Takes exporters to international trade fairs and exhibitions. (6) Legal assistance: Helps with trade disputes and payment recovery in some cases. Website: https://www.fieo.org. Membership: Open to Indian exporters; annual membership fee applies.
source_name: FIEO — Federation of Indian Export Organisations

influence a country's GDP, exchange rate, level of inflation as well as interest rates.
A robust export data is beneficial as it leads to increase in job opportunities,
enhances foreign currency reserves, boosts manufacturing and also increases
government's revenue collection. It is also a good means by which a country can bring
itself out of the recession phase.
Exporting to countries with a favourable economic climate helps in increasing
the GDP levels as well as helps in reducing unemployment.
Entering international markets is a long and complex process that requires
companies/entrepreneurs to allocate numerous resources in terms of time and
money. However, it is a rewarding effort because exporting is also the fastest way to
internationalise a company / business -a strategy that facilitates long-term

obtaining an import license from the relevant regional licensing authority. The goods
covered by the license shall be disposed of in the manner specified by the license
authority, which should be clearly indicated in the license itself. The list of restricted
goods is provided in ITC (HS). An import license is valid for 24 months for capital
goods, and 18 months for all other goods
Canalized Items - Canalized goods are items which may only be imported using
specific procedures or methods of transport. The list of canalized goods can be found
in the ITC (HS). Goods in this category can be imported only through canalizing
agencies. The main canalized items are currently petroleum products, bulk
agricultural products, such as grains and vegetable oils, and some pharmaceutical
products.

India FTA Engagements
India has signed 13 free trade agreements (FTAs) and 6 preferential trade
agreements (PTA). In the Indian context, the key differences between an FTA and a
PTA are that the FTA is comprehensive across a number of areas and has deeper
commitments while a PTA is confined to trade in goods and seeks only tariff
elimination in terms of a margin of preference (MOP). Moreover, the coverage of a PTA
on goods is also limited as compared to an FTA. Knowledge about concessions given
by the other nations to india in exports and imports will be beneficial to Indian
exporters to utilize that concessions and considerations.

Incoterms are the selling terms that the buyer and seller of goods both agree
to during international transactions. These rules are accepted by governments and
legal authorities around the world. Understanding Incoterms is a vital part of
International Trade because they clearly state which tasks, costs and risks are
associated with the buyer and the seller.

SPS Agreement (Sanitary and Phytosanitary):
The Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary
Measures (the "SPS Agreement") entered into force with the establishment of the World
Trade Organization on 1 January 1995. It concerns the application of food safety and
animal and plant health regulations.
Introduction:
The Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary
Measures sets out the basic rules for food safety and animal and plant health
standards.
It allows countries to set their own standards. But it also says regulations
must be based on science. They should be applied only to the extent necessary to
protect human, animal or plant life or health. And they should not arbitrarily or
unjustifiably discriminate between countries where identical or similar conditions
prevail.
Member countries are encouraged to use international standards, guidelines
and recommendations where they exist. However, members may use measures which
result in higher standards if there is scientific justification. They can also set higher
standards based on appropriate assessment of risks so long as the approach is
consistent, not arbitrary.
The agreement still allows countries to use different standards and different
methods of inspecting products.

Remission of Duties or Taxes on Export Products Scheme (RoDTEP)
RoDTEP stands for the Remission of Duties or Taxes on Export Products Scheme.
The scheme has been introduced with an objective to neutralize the taxes and duties
suffered on exported goods which are otherwise not credited or remitted or refunded in
any manner and remain embedded in the export goods. This scheme provides for
rebate of all hidden Central, State, and Local duties/taxes/levies on the goods
exported which have not been refunded under any other existing scheme. This does
not only include the direct cost incurred by the exporter but also the prior stage
cumulative indirect taxes on goods. It is a WTO compliant Scheme and follows the
global principle that the taxes/duties should not be exported; they should be either
exempted or remitted to exporters, to make the goods competitive in the global market.
The RoDTEP scheme has been made effective for the exports from 1st January 2021.

BRC Certification:
A bank issues a Bank Realisation Certificate (BRC) as proof that an exporter
has received money from an importer for the exported goods. Exporters should report
to the bank the value of the goods that they intend to export. The banks will record
the export transactions on the Export Data Processing and Monitoring System
(EDPMS). When the exporters receive payments, they should submit all shipping bills
with the banks. They banks will cancel the items recorded in the EDPMS and issue an
e-BRC against the shipping bill payments.
An exporter requires a BRC to avail of the different export incentives offered
by the government, such as subsidies, low-cost loans, duty exemptions, etc., as part of
its FTP.
Before the introduction of e-BRC, exporters had to go to their banks and
apply for the issue of a BRC. The exporters submitted the BRC to the Directorate
General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) regional authority, and the transaction details of the
exports were entered manually according to the BRC. It was a time-consuming which
complicated the process of claiming export incentives.

Importers and Exporters. This document will act as the user guide for Importer and Exporter working on
the e-RCMC module available on https://www.dgft.gov.in.

Soft Launch of Electronic Filing of Registration Cum Membership Certificate (RCMC) / Registration
Certificate (RC) through the Common Digital Platform w.e.f. 6 December 2021 vide Trade Notice
No. 27/2021-2022 Dated 30.11.2021.
Transition Period of 3 Months i.e., up to Feb. 2022 or until further orders.
Electronic (Paper less & contact less) and Real-Time Issuance of Certificate.
Single Source of Information – IEC Details are auto-authenticated and common across the Trade
Ecosystem.
CBDT and MCA Integration in-built in the System – For PAN/DIN Details Auto-validation in
Exporters IEC Profile.
Auto-generation of Invoice by the System.

Registration-Cum-Membership Certificate (RCMC) is a certificate that validates an exporter
dealing with products registered with an agency/ organization that are authorized by the Indian
Government.
While applying for RCMC, an exporter has to declare his main line of business in the application.
The exporter is required to obtain RCMC from the Council which is concerned with the product of
his main line of business.

Only users with RCMC issued earlier shall be able to apply for renewal of the RCMC. RCMC
details would be available in system and prepopulated in the form as per the application at the

Promotion Mission (EPM), aimed at expanding global market access and enhancing the
competitiveness of Indian exporters, particularly Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs).
Building on the interventions that were already supporting exporters, the Government has now
launched 7 additional interventions under EPM, significantly expanding the scope of support
across trade finance, compliance enablement, logistics and overseas market access. With this
expansion, 10 interventions under the Mission are now operational, marking a major milestone
in the rollout of EPM and reinforcing India’s commitment to inclusive and export-led growth.

What is the Export Promotion Mission?
The Export Promotion Mission (EPM) is a flagship initiative designed to provide coordinated support
across key elements of the export ecosystem, including trade finance, standards compliance, logistics,
overseas warehousing and market development.
Approved by the Government in November 2025, the Mission brings together multiple export-
support measures under a single, unified and digitally driven framework. With a total outlay of
₹25,060 crore for the period FY 2025–26 to FY 2030–31, EPM seeks to enhance export
competitiveness and expand India’s global presence.

[Page 2]
The Mission is implemented through two integrated sub-schemes: Niryat Protsahan, which
focuses on financial enablers and trade-finance support, and Niryat Disha, which addresses non-
financial, market-access and ecosystem enablers.
Through this framework, the Export Promotion Mission aims to:
• Improve access to affordable and diversified trade finance, particularly for MSMEs and first-
time exporters
• Support compliance with international quality, technical and sustainability standards
• Strengthen export branding, logistics and overseas warehousing capabilities
• Expand market access and trade intelligence support
• Enable broader participation of MSMEs, including growth of cross-border e-commerce

Procedure for Application
Niryat Protsahan
For Niryat Protsahan interventions, exporters file an Intent-to-Claim (IC) on dgft.gov.in prior to
obtaining support, upon which a Unique Identification Number (UIN) is generated. The exporter
shares the UIN with the lending institution or factoring entity. Lending institutions extend the credit
or trade finance instruments to exporters and submit the Claim Submission (CS) to the
implementing agency as per notified guidelines.

[Page 9]
Niryat Disha
For LIFT and TRACE, exporters file an Intent-to-Claim (IC) on trade.gov.in before obtaining EXIM-
related services and submit a Reimbursement Claim (RC) after export completion with supporting
documents and self-certification.
For FLOW, INSIGHT and MAS, assistance is provided through a proposal-based approval mechanism,
with applications submitted on trade.gov.in, followed by evaluation by the EPM Division,
recommendation by the Sub-Committee and final approval by the Steering Committee.

financial institutions, Export Promotion Councils and Indian Missions abroad, EPM is envisaged
to promote inclusive, decentralised and sustainable export growth.
